stem.text: Neurones in the brain metabolise glucose to produce ATP. Glucose enters brain neurones through transport proteins in the cell surface membrane. These proteins are similar to the transport proteins for glucose found in liver and muscle cells.
State the process by which glucose passes through transport proteins into brain neurones.

explanation.text: A carrier can transport glucose down its concentration gradient without using ATP. Protein involvement alone does not make a transport process active.

reasoningChain: Use the direction down the concentration gradient.

stem.text: Brain neurones use ATP very quickly.
One brain neurone uses 4.7 × 10<sup>9</sup> molecules of ATP per second.
One striated muscle cell uses 9.8 × 10<sup>6</sup> molecules of ATP per second.
Calculate how many muscle cells would use the same number of ATP molecules per second as one brain neurone.
Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

points.text: 480 ; max 1 if not as a whole number 479.5918367 If standard form incorrect allow max 1 if evidence of 4.7 divided 9.8

explanation.text: Divide the ATP demand of one neurone by the demand of one muscle cell. Handling the powers of ten separately gives (4.7 / 9.8) × 10<sup>3</sup>, about 480 cells.

reasoningChain: Form the ratio of neurone demand to muscle-cell demand.
Evaluate and round to the nearest whole cell.

inferredMistakes.text: Dividing muscle-cell ATP use by neurone ATP use, giving the reciprocal of the required cell number.

explanation.text: Neurones must continually maintain ion gradients as well as synthesise and release signalling molecules. ATP powers pumps, biosynthesis and vesicle transport; ion diffusion through an open channel does not itself consume ATP.

reasoningChain: Identify energy-requiring activities in the neurone.
Connect each activity to a named use of ATP.

stem.text: When ATP is completely broken down, the compound adenosine is released which then leaves the cell.

items: During the day, the extracellular concentration of adenosine increases.
In brain synapses, adenosine binds to adenosine receptors in the cell surface membrane of postsynaptic brain neurones and inhibits postsynaptic neurone activity.
During sleep, adenosine detaches from its receptor and is recycled to form ATP.
This action promotes wakefulness (the person is awake).

stem.text: Caffeine is a compound found naturally in tea and coffee and is added to some drinks. Caffeine has a similar shape to adenosine.
Suggest and explain the effect on the sleep pattern of a person who has had a drink containing a lot of caffeine.

points.text: (caffeine) binds to (adenosine) receptors ; R active site or inhibits / blocks, binding of adenosine to receptors / AW ;
less ATP made during sleep / more ATP made whilst awake ;
postsynaptic (neurone) activity is not inhibited / can occur / AW ;
(less adenosine bound to receptors) cannot promote sleep / promotes wakefulness / AW ;

explanation.text: Caffeine can compete with adenosine for its receptor because of its similar shape. Blocking adenosine’s inhibitory effect maintains postsynaptic activity and can delay sleep.

reasoningChain: Trace reduced adenosine action to altered neuronal activity and sleep.
